messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm: calculate values of terms for given network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ergm: calculate values of terms for given network
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

The ergm package supports a number of "terms" that can be used to construct ERG models.  Is there any functionality in statnet that will let me calculate the values of these "terms" for a given network?

For example, we have the terms 'edges', 'triangle', 'gwdsp'.  Are there corresponding functions for calculating the number of edges, triangles, GWDSP(?) for a given network object?

If I'm correct, the internally ergm package is only using changes of these quantities when a single edge is added or removed from the graph.  Are there any utility functions for the convenience of users that can calculate these quantities though, at least the ones that are supported out of the box?

Szabolcs

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Basic modeling of medical facts
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am new to network modeling and am trying to figure out if the data I have is suitable for use in ERGM, or if some transformation of it would be.

I have medical history data on millions of people.  From this data, I computed a network where nodes are conditions and a link (i,j) indicates the number of people who had condition i prior to condition j. The conditions are summarized into roughly 500 conditions.  For each link I can define the probability of of the link (i,j) from the observed data (number of people who have j after i / number with i ), or a suitable weight for the strength of the association.

I can analyse this network assuming the edge weights are deterministic but that hasn't been very fruitful so far. I am not sure ERGM applies because all the examples I see involve unweighted edges.

I think I need to look into bnlearn or other Bayesian networks, but wanted to check here to see if there are any ideas on how to apply ERGM to this type of data.

Thanks,
Chris

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Basic modeling of medical facts
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 9 Oct 2013, Hane, Christopher A wrote:

Hi Chris,

> I have medical history data on millions of people.? From this data, I computed a network where nodes are conditions
> and a link (i,j) indicates the number of people who had condition i prior to condition j. The conditions are
> summarized into roughly 500 conditions.? For each link I can define the probability of of the link (i,j) from the
> observed data (number of people who have j after i / number with i ), or a suitable weight for the strength of the
> association.

This is a fascinating use of network analysis -- it reminds me of a 
similar approach to modeling the occupational structure, using job titles 
as nodes, and people's job changes as links or link weights.

Note that you could also treat this as a 2 mode network: persons and 
conditions.  That would remove the temporal ordering, but would pick up 
clustering.

> I can analyse this network assuming the edge weights are deterministic but that hasn?t been very fruitful so far. I am
> not sure ERGM applies because all the examples I see involve unweighted edges.

You're in luck, if you call being first in line lucky.  Pavel Krivitsky 
has developed the theory, methods and code for analyzing networks with 
valued/weighted edges.  He taught a workshop on this at the Sunbelt 
meetings last May in Hamburg, and the materials from that tutorial are 
here:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2013/Valued.pdf
(all the tutorial materials are on the Sunbelt2013 page)

and the paper is here:

Pavel~N. Krivitsky. Exponential-family random graph models for valued 
networks. Electronic Journal of Statistics, 6:1100{1128, 2012. doi: 
10.1214/12-EJS696.

The key issue in valued ties is how to aggregate the values into the 
statistics that will be used in the model to represent processes of 
interest.  For binary ties, we typically use sums and sums of products, 
which is pretty simple.  With valued ties there is both the question of 
what summary (mean, max, min, sum, etc.) and what distributional 
assumptions to make for inference.

Take a look at the tutorial materials and let us know what you think.

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Need help with an error
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I apologize if this is on the forum, but in my scan I'm not seeing it. And this might be a question with a really obvious answer.

I am fitting a very simple ergm model (basically of the form "model_name <- ergm(network_name ~ triangle)"), and I get the following error:

"Number of edges in a simulated network exceeds that in the observed by a factor of more than 20. This is a strong indicator of model degeneracy. If you are reasonably certain that this is not the case, increase the MCMLE.density.guard control.ergm() parameter."

So how exactly do I increase the MCMLE.density.guard control.ergm() parameter? I tried "model_name <- ergm(network_name ~ triangle, MCMLE.density.guard=large_number)", but I got the same error again. There must be something more to it, but I'm so bad at R that I can't figure it out.

Thanks,
Vicki Hertzberg

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicki.

I think you should try including an "edges" term before altering software
parameters. The edges term controls for the observed number of edges. It's
much like an intercept term, except it isn't included by default. There
could be more to that story...

Nathan Doogan

messages.body_plain:
Vicki,

You are trying to fit a model that is the cannonical example of a model 
that is almost always degenerate.  There is a great deal written on the 
problem of degeneracy when using this kind of homogenous reduced Markov 
model.  There's some discussion of it in the ERGM tutorial on the statnet 
wiki:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2013#WorkshopMaterials

A more thorough discussion here:

NEW SPECIFICATIONS FOR EXPONENTIAL RANDOM GRAPH MODELS
Tom A. B. Snijders1, Philippa E. Pattison2, Garry L. Robins2, Mark S. 
Handcock3
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2006.00176.x/abstract

And a good technical discussion is found here:

Mark S Handcock
?Assessing Degeneracy in Statistical Models of Social Networks?
http://www.csss.washington.edu/Papers/wp39.ps

The alternative is to use the gwesp term to capture triad closure instead. 
You can read about that in this paper:

Goodreau S, Kitts J, Morris M: Birds of a Feather, or Friend of a 
Friend? Using Statistical Network Analysis to Investigate Adolescent 
Social Networks. Demography 2009, 46(1):103?125.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Martina!

Sent from my iPhone

> On Oct 10, 2013, at 1:57 PM, "martina morris" <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:
> 
> Vicki,
> 
> You are trying to fit a model that is the cannonical example of a model that is almost always degenerate.  There is a great deal written on the problem of degeneracy when using this kind of homogenous reduced Markov model.  There's some discussion of it in the ERGM tutorial on the statnet wiki:
> 
> https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2013#WorkshopMaterials
> 
> A more thorough discussion here:
> 
> NEW SPECIFICATIONS FOR EXPONENTIAL RANDOM GRAPH MODELS
> Tom A. B. Snijders1, Philippa E. Pattison2, Garry L. Robins2, Mark S. Handcock3
> http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2006.00176.x/abstract
> 
> And a good technical discussion is found here:
> 
> Mark S Handcock
> ?Assessing Degeneracy in Statistical Models of Social Networks?
> http://www.csss.washington.edu/Papers/wp39.ps
> 
> The alternative is to use the gwesp term to capture triad closure instead. You can read about that in this paper:
> 
> Goodreau S, Kitts J, Morris M: Birds of a Feather, or Friend of a Friend? Using Statistical Network Analysis to Investigate Adolescent Social Networks. Demography 2009, 46(1):103?125.
> 
>> On Thu, 10 Oct 2013, Hertzberg, Vicki S wrote:
>> 
>> Thanks to Zane I was able to "sort of" get this to work. Nathan indicated that I needed an edges term. I knew that but
>> wanted to keep my request as simple as possible. Now I have another problem.
>> Now it works fine with no "edges" term (I.e., only the triangle term), but increasing parameters in the control. I
>> don't have to monkey with the parameters to do just an edges term. However, when I try edges+triangle on the following
>> statement:
>> model7 <- ergm(billavf2 ~ edges + triangle, control = control.ergm(MCMLE.density.guard.min = 400000,
>> MCMLE.density.guard = exp(3))
>> + )
>> I get the following error:
>> Error in if (order) coefs[order, seq_len(order)] else numeric() :
>>   argument is not interpretable as logical
>> In addition: Warning message:
>> In if (order) coefs[order, seq_len(order)] else numeric() :
>>   the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
>> I'm not sure I can even decipher this. Any thoughts?
>> Thanks
>> Vicki
>> From: ND <doogan.1@osu.edu>
>> Date: Thursday, October 10, 2013 12:53 PM
>> To: mememe Hertzberg <vhertzb@emory.edu>

>> Hi Vicki.
>> I think you should try including an "edges" term before altering software parameters. The edges term controls for the

>> Nathan Doogan

>> I am fitting a very simple ergm model (basically of the form "model_name <- ergm(network_name ~ triangle)"), and

>> "Number of edges in a simulated network exceeds that in the observed by a factor of more than 20. This is a
>> strong indicator of model degeneracy. If you are reasonably certain that this is not the case, increase the
